podcast.title: Conflict with Sire Over Singles (1985)
podcast.body: Geffen executives bickered with Sire Records over which Madonna songs from the "Vision Quest" soundtrack could be released as singles. As a result of a compromise, Geffen issued "Crazy for You" as a 45. "They compromised, and Crazy for you was issued by Geffen as a 45."

podcast.title: Post-1989 Grunge Expansion
podcast.body: After 1989, as grunge became more popular, the movement began to expand from Sub Pop to Geffen, with the most commercially successful acts moving to the major label. "Justo después ya todo el movimiento granch, saldría de su pop a Giffen."

podcast.title: Questionable Practices (1992-1994)
podcast.body: Although considered an independent label, Geffen Records exhibited "quite questionable behavior" with some grunge artists between 1992 and 1994. They sometimes acted like a large multinational, over-exposing, over-exploiting, and pressuring artists heavily for commercial gain. "Geffen aunque era una discurreficia independiente siempre tuvo un comportamiento bastante cuestionable con algunos artistas de gran serie entre el 92 y el 94."

podcast.title: First Major Label Internet Distribution (1994)
podcast.body: In 1994, Geffen Records made history by issuing Aerosmith's B-side "Head First" for free on Compuserve. This was the first instance of a major label distributing a song over the internet, serving as an early "beta test" for digital music dissemination, despite the slow dial-up speeds of the time. "Geffen Records issued an Erasmith B-side called Head First for free on the then dominant internet service provider Compuserve."

podcast.title: "Mother" of the Grunge Movement
podcast.body: Geffen Records is described as the "absolute mother" of the grunge movement, playing an immensely significant role in shaping the sound of American rock. The grunge movement itself developed within the label in the late 1980s. "Giffen que es la madra absoluta del movimiento grancho y este movimiento discográfico es muchísimo más importante de lo que parece para definir el sonido del rock de Estados Unidos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: SONIC YOUTH: Guitarras al límite

podcast.title: Artist-Friendly Contract Release
podcast.body: Despite a six-album contract, Geffen Records ultimately chose to release Sloan from their contractual obligations, which the band found to be an "artist friendly and cool" decision, especially as Geffen was financially secure and "didn't really need us." This allowed Sloan to pursue other labels and eventually regain their music rights. "But in the end, Geffen was just cool. Like, first of all, they don't need, they made tons of money so they didn't really need us. But they were really artist friendly and cool. And they said, just go, we're not going to hold you to contract."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Attempted Suede Signing
podcast.body: Geffen, described as one of the "mothers of the grunge movement" (a major label in the grunge scene), attempted to sign Suede after their rapid rise to prominence and their Melody Maker cover in 1991, but Suede rejected their powerful contract offers. "la discórafica Gifen, que era una de las magres del movimiento granch intentó fichar a Swade."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: SUEDE: Pilares del Brit Pop

podcast.title: Cross-Pollination with Sonic Youth
podcast.body: The signing of Sonic Youth to Geffen Records was highly influential. Sonic Youth's sound permeated the grunge albums being made at Geffen, and conversely, Sonic Youth absorbed fresh ideas from the younger grunge bands also working there, which helped to update their sound significantly during the 1990s. This interaction profoundly nourished American rock. "ese tan de en que hizo que Sonidjuz se entreme clase con bandas del grancho en la discográfica Giffen, nutrió muchísimo todo el rock americano."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: SONIC YOUTH: Guitarras al límite

podcast.title: Dropped Lock Up
podcast.body: Geffen Records initially signed Tom Morello's band, Lock Up, and released their album "Something Bitchin This Way Comes" in 1989. However, due to the album's commercial failure, the label decided to drop the band by early 1991. "Actually that first record was a flop, so they were dropped by their record label."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rage Against The Machine: Part 1

podcast.title: Formation of DGC Subsidiary
podcast.body: Geffen Records, a major label, created a brand new subsidiary label called DGC. This decision was driven by the desire to sign Sonic Youth, who were playing hard to get, and to establish an "alternative label" that would be distributed by Geffen but run with the attitude and aesthetic of an indie label. "So a representative from Geffen Records convinced the bosses to create a brand new subsidiary label called DGC."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8

podcast.title: Involvement in Kurt Cobain's Intervention
podcast.body: Executives from Geffen, Nirvana's record label, participated in the drug intervention organized for Kurt Cobain on March 25, 1994, to address his heroin problem. "se juntan a unos directivos de su discográfica de Geffen, se juntan dos de sus mejores amigos para hablar del problema que tiene Kurt Cobain con las drogas, sobre todo con Aeroina."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: El secreto de La muerte de Kurt Cobain

podcast.title: Mainstream Grunge Label
podcast.body: Geffen Records became a destination for grunge bands after their initial development on independent labels like Sub Pop, particularly as the movement gained global recognition. Nirvana, for example, eventually moved from Sub Pop to Geffen. "nacen el supo para luego saltar a Geffen."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cuál fue el primer disco de Grunge?

podcast.title: Nirvana's Label
podcast.body: Geffen Records was the label for the iconic grunge band Nirvana. Sloan signed with Geffen in 1992 for their "Smeared" album, at the height of the grunge era, in an attempt to break into the American market. "They were signed to Nirvana's label, the height of the whole Grunge thing, but eventually that whole thing fell apart largely due to some label politics and they were dropped."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Parent Label of DGC
podcast.body: Geffen Records is the major label parent company of DGC Records, which was the label responsible for releasing Nirvana's highly successful "Nevermind" album. "DGC Records, a subsidiary of Major Label Geffen Records."

podcast.title: Refusal to Release Rivers Cuomo's Solo Material
podcast.body: Geffen Records refused to release Rivers Cuomo's home recordings, later compiled in the "Alone" series, for years. They believed that "substandard material" would sully the good name of Weezer, though Rivers eventually won the right to release them in 2007. "Geffen refused to release that material for years because they didn't want substandard material sullying the good name of Weezer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rivers Cuomo and Weezer - Alt-Rock's Nerd Heroes Part 1

podcast.title: Released Death to False Metal
podcast.body: Weezer returned to Geffen for the release of "Death to False Metal," after "Hurley" was released on Epitaph Records. "For the next record, they were back on Geffen."

podcast.title: Relevant Discographic Movement
podcast.body: The interactions and developments at Geffen Records, particularly concerning the grunge movement and Sonic Youth, represent one of the most relevant and impactful discographic movements in the history of rock music. "este es increíblemente relevante, son unos los movimientos discográficos más relevantes del rock."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: SONIC YOUTH: Guitarras al límite

podcast.title: Skepticism Towards "Twice Removed"
podcast.body: Geffen Records expressed significant concern about Sloan's album "Twice Removed" due to its stylistic departure from "Smeared," viewing it as a completely different band and suggesting they "redo the whole thing" because it would be difficult to market. Despite this, Sloan stood their ground, a move that later became part of their "sticking it to the man" narrative. "It is true that Geffen, when they heard it, they were like, what are you serious? Like, this is a different band. It's going to be hard for us to market you. Please, you know, consider redoing the whole thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Sloan's First Album Remix
podcast.body: Geffen Records picked up Sloan's first record (later known as "Smeared") and remixed it for distribution. This remix cost $1,200. "The first record we made, which was on Gephin, we made with the aspirations of trying to make a thousand CDs or five hundred. And then we got picked up and remixed by Gephin."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Sloan's Major Label Deal
podcast.body: Geffen Records (also referred to as DGC) signed Sloan after A&R representative Todd Sullivan was captivated by their song "Underwhelmed." The signing was a rapid and exciting event for the Halifax band. "He set it to a friend of his Todd Sullivanic Geffen who loved the song underwhelmed and then came to see his play and then he was like, do you guys want to sign to Geffen?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Weezer Signing
podcast.body: Weezer signed a deal with Geffen Records on June 25, 1993, after considerable pushback from the label's bosses regarding the band's choice of producer, Ric Ocasek. "Weezer signed a deal on June 25, 1993."
